summary: Updates RFC 6775 and RFC 8505 to enable proxy services for IPv6 Neighbor Discovery by Routing Registrars called Backbone Routers. They sit along the wireless edge of a backbone and join several wireless links into one multi-link subnet. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery finds the owner of an address by sending a message that a wireless link turns into a broadcast, so every device nearby has to receive it. RFC 8929 puts a router at the edge of the wireless network that answers for the small devices, so several wireless links can share one IP subnet without flooding the radio.

subtitle: Backbone routers that answer IPv6 Neighbor Discovery on behalf of wireless nodes, so several wireless links can act as one subnet.

tldr.problem: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery relies on multicast, which a wireless link typically turns into a broadcast. That wastes bandwidth and battery, and duplicate address detection often fails on wireless.
tldr.mechanism: Nodes register their addresses with a 6LoWPAN Backbone Router (6BBR) using the registration extension from RFC 8505. The 6BBR keeps a Binding Table and does the Neighbor Discovery on the backbone for them, either as a Routing Proxy or as a Bridging Proxy.
tldr.outcome: Several wireless links plus a backbone can be federated into one Multi-Link Subnet without flooding the wireless side. The scheme still needs the backbone, and every router on it, to be trusted.

today: RFC 8929 was published in November 2020 and is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 6775 and RFC 8505, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Wireless Links Need a Proxy
sections.content:
Ethernet bridging gives wired networks an efficient broadcast service, and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (ND) was designed around it. On Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs) and local wireless networks, multicast is typically broadcast on the radio, so a Neighbor Solicitation sent to a Solicited-Node Multicast Address reaches most wireless nodes anyway. That can consume enough bandwidth to degrade the unicast traffic service, and it forces battery-powered nodes to keep their radios on so that they can listen.

Duplicate Address Detection (DAD) also often fails to find duplicates over wireless, because broadcast is unreliable there. The RFC notes that IPv6 addresses rarely conflict mostly because of the entropy of 64-bit Interface IDs, not because DAD works well.

The answer is a Multi-Link Subnet (MLSN): each link, including the backbone, is its own broadcast domain, but they share one subnet. This RFC defines Neighbor Discovery proxies called 6LoWPAN Backbone Routers (6BBRs) at the boundary between the wireless links and the backbone. It updates RFC 6775 and RFC 8505.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbor Discovery asks who holds a given address by sending a message that a wireless link turns into a broadcast, so every nearby device has to receive it. That wastes bandwidth and battery, and the check for a duplicate address often fails. A router at the edge of the wireless network takes that work over for the small devices.

sections.title: The Roles and the Registration Fields
sections.content:
The RFC uses a small set of role names. A 6LoWPAN Node (6LN) is a device on the wireless link. A 6LoWPAN Router (6LR) is a router on that link. A 6LoWPAN Border Router (6LBR) connects the wireless network to the backbone, and a 6LoWPAN Backbone Router (6BBR) sits on the backbone and provides the Neighbor Discovery proxy service.

Three fields carry the registration state. The Extended Address Registration Option (EARO) is the option a node attaches to its Neighbor Solicitation to register an address. Inside it, the Registration Ownership Verifier (ROVR) identifies the owner of the address, so a duplicate registration and a moved registration can be told apart. The Transaction ID (TID) orders registrations, so the freshest one wins.

A Binding is one entry in a 6BBR's Binding Table, the database of registrations the router holds. The combined Binding Tables of all the 6BBRs on a backbone form a distributed database of the registered nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC names four roles: the small device, the router next to it on the wireless link, the border router, and the backbone router that does the answering. Each registration carries an owner tag and a counter, so the router can tell a duplicate from a move and can tell which registration is the newest.

sections.title: How a Node Registers Its Address
sections.content:
Rather than working out which addresses to proxy by watching the Neighbor Discovery traffic, which the RFC says has proved unreliable, the address is signalled explicitly. A 6LN registers all of its IPv6 addresses with its 6LR by sending a Neighbor Solicitation carrying an EARO with the R flag set, as specified in RFC 8505. If the 6LR is a 6BBR, the 6LN is both the Registered Node and the Registering Node. Otherwise the 6LBR proxies the registration on the node's behalf, and the 6LBR is the Registering Node.

The 6BBR then performs Neighbor Discovery on its backbone interface for the registered addresses, with no broadcast over the wireless medium. Two topologies are covered: an access link such as Wi-Fi, where the 6BBR can sit in the access point, and a route-over mesh, where the 6LBR is the root of the mesh and registers the addresses to the 6BBR.

An address may be registered to more than one 6BBR for availability. The primary 6BBR is the one with the highest 64-bit EUI-64 address among those sharing the same registration, compared as an unsigned 64-bit integer. If a Registering Node loses a 6BBR, it MUST increment the TID when it re-registers, which forces the state to move to the new 6BBR.
sections.plainLanguage: Each device tells its nearest router which addresses it owns, using a solicitation with a registration option. The backbone router writes them down and answers for those devices whenever anyone on the backbone asks. A device that moves to another backbone router raises a counter, so the old router hands over the entry.

sections.title: Multi-Link Subnet Rules and the Optional Border Router
sections.content:
The backbone and the federated wireless links are different links in the multi-link subnet, and Neighbor Discovery messages are link-scoped, so a 6BBR does not forward them between links. Legacy hosts on the backbone assume that the subnet sits inside one link and will not run Path MTU Discovery for a destination in the subnet. So the MTU MUST be the same on the backbone and on all federated wireless links, and the 6BBR MUST use the same MTU value in the Router Advertisements on both sides. Link-local traffic, link-scope multicast and traffic with a hop limit of 1 do not cross between links.

A 6LBR can optionally serve the whole subnet. When one is present, the 6BBR checks with it using an Extended Duplicate Address Request and Confirmation exchange, whether a new registration is a duplicate or a move, before running duplicate address detection. The 6LBR answers with status 1 (Duplicate Address), 3 (Moved) or 0 (Success). Because other hosts on the backbone may not be registered, the 6BBR still runs duplicate address detection afterwards.

A Registering Node MUST implement RFC 8505 and register all of its addresses, because an unregistered address may become unreachable. A prefix used across the subnet MAY be advertised as on-link over the backbone for compatibility with existing IPv6 hosts, and MUST NOT be advertised as on-link toward the wireless link in Routing Proxy mode.
sections.plainLanguage: All the links in the subnet must use the same maximum packet size, because older hosts on the backbone will not discover it for themselves. An optional border router can keep the master list of addresses and tell a backbone router whether a new registration is a duplicate or a move.

sections.title: The Routing Proxy
sections.content:
A Routing Proxy provides Neighbor Discovery proxy functions for Global and Unique Local Addresses between the LLN and the backbone, but not for link-local addresses. It operates as an IPv6 border router with full link-layer isolation, and it installs a connected host route to the registered address, via the Registering Node identified by the source address and the SLLAO in the registration message.

In this mode the 6BBR MUST use its own Layer 2 address on the backbone interface in the SLLAO of the Router Solicitation messages and the TLLAO of the Neighbor Advertisement messages it generates. The link-layer addresses of the 6LNs are therefore not visible at Layer 2 on the backbone. The mode is required when the LLN uses a different link-layer address format from the backbone, such as EUI-64 against EUI-48, and it is also useful when the Layer 2 topology is virtualized over a wide area.

When a registered address moves to another 6BBR, the previous 6BBR SHOULD send a gratuitous Neighbor Advertisement to each backbone peer that cached its link-layer address, supplying the new 6BBR's address. If a peer misses it, the previous 6BBR looks the address up again and forwards the packet to the right 6BBR, and SHOULD also send a redirect message to update the peer's cache.
sections.plainLanguage: In routing proxy mode the backbone router answers under its own link-layer address and routes the packets itself. The wireless devices' link-layer addresses never appear on the backbone, which is what makes the mode work when the two sides use different address formats.

sections.title: The Bridging Proxy
sections.content:
A Bridging Proxy provides Neighbor Discovery proxy functions while preserving forwarding continuity at the link layer. It acts as a Layer 2 bridge for all types of unicast packets, including link-scoped ones, and appears as an IPv6 host on the backbone.

In this mode the 6BBR MUST use the Registering Node's Layer 2 address, taken from the SLLAO of the registration message, in the SLLAO of the Neighbor Solicitation and Router Solicitation messages and the TLLAO of the Neighbor Advertisements it generates. It proxies Neighbor Discovery for all unicast addresses including link-local ones, and it preferably forwards lookup and reachability messages to the Registering Node as unicast frames, so that the node answers for itself.

Classical Neighbor Discovery on the backbone is not disabled by this scheme. A node that receives several Neighbor Advertisements updates an existing neighbor cache entry only if the Override flag is set; otherwise it probes the cached address. Nodes on the backbone SHOULD support RFC 7048, which makes the reachability check less impatient, because movement with a slow reattachment can otherwise time out too quickly.
sections.plainLanguage: In bridging proxy mode the backbone router uses the device's own link-layer address, so the device keeps its identity as it moves between access points. It also forwards lookups to the device when it can, so that the device answers for itself.

sections.title: The Binding Table and Its Three States
sections.content:
Each 6BBR keeps a Binding Table. A Binding holds the registered address, information about the Registering Node such as its connecting interface, link-local address and link-layer address, the EARO with its ROVR and TID, and a state. The state is Tentative, Reachable or Stale.

  • Tentative: duplicate address detection is running over the backbone for TENTATIVE_DURATION. A conflicting Neighbor Advertisement or NS(DAD) with a different ROVR removes the Binding, and the Registering Node is told status 1 (Duplicate Address). When the timer elapses the Binding becomes Reachable and the Registering Node gets status 0 (Success).
  • Reachable: an active registration. Lookups and reachability checks SHOULD be answered with the Override flag not set. A fresher registration for the same ROVR removes the Binding and returns status 4 (Removed). An older one is answered with status 3 (Moved). When the Registration Lifetime ends, the Binding becomes Stale.
  • Stale: the 6BBR does not defend the address, but it tracks the backbone peers that still point to it. Before answering a lookup it MUST first run a reachability check to the Registering Node. When STALE_DURATION elapses, the Binding MUST be removed.

The ROVR separates duplication from movement: a different ROVR means a different owner, and the same ROVR with a different TID means the same owner moved.
sections.plainLanguage: The router's list has three kinds of entry: just arrived and being checked for duplicates, active, and possibly gone. In the third state the router checks with the device before it answers for it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The scheme assumes that each wireless link is protected against rogue access, and that the backbone is physically secured so that packets can neither be forged nor overheard. The wireless link layer must provide secure unicast to and from the backbone router and secure broadcast from the routers, in a way that prevents tampering with or replaying the Neighbor Discovery messages.

For Neighbor Discovery over the backbone, and unless classical ND is disabled by configuration, the classical messages are interpreted as coming from the address owner and take precedence over the 6BBR, which is only a proxy. The threats listed in Section 11.1 of RFC 4861 therefore apply in full: any node on the backbone can claim any address, including those of wireless nodes, by sending a Neighbor Advertisement with the Override bit set, and the real owner stops receiving its packets. Such a node can also forge traffic, present itself as a preferred router, and snoop what it intercepts. Rogue access to the backbone must therefore be prevented at all times, and attached nodes must be fully trusted.

Coupling address registration with RFC 8928 proves address ownership on the wireless link through the ROVR field, but that protection does not extend over the backbone, because the 6BBR cannot provide the proof of ownership when it defends the address. An attacker on the backbone can send a Neighbor Solicitation with an EARO, learn the TID and ROVR from the reply, raise the TID and take over the Binding. Compromised 6BBRs, 6LBRs and 6LRs are also attack points, so all of them must be trusted.
sections.plainLanguage: This design only works if everyone on the backbone is trusted. A node that can send packets there can claim any address and read the traffic sent to it. The registration proof protects the wireless link, but not the backbone.
